title: Did Eating Potatoes Give Some People a Superpower?
summary: Have you ever wondered why some people can eat tons of potatoes and feel great? Scientists just found a clue hidden in our genes! A new study shows that Indigenous people in the Peruvian Andes have a special genetic superpower: they carry more copies of a gene called AMY1. This gene helps your body make an enzyme in your spit that starts breaking down starchy foods like potatoes right in your mouth. Thousands of years ago, the ancestors of these Andean people started farming potatoes. Potatoes are packed with starch, so being able to digest them well was a big advantage. Over many generations, people with more AMY1 copies were healthier and had more kids. Those with fewer copies slowly disappeared from the population. It's like evolution was sculpting a statue, chipping away the parts that didn't fit. Today, Indigenous Peruvians have an average of 10 AMY1 copies—that's two to four more than any other group studied! To make sure potatoes were the real reason, scientists compared them with the Maya people in Mexico, who share ancient roots but didn't farm potatoes. The Maya average only 6 copies. This difference strongly suggests that a diet rich in potatoes shaped human evolution in the Andes. So next time you eat a french fry, remember: for some people, potatoes are more than just food—they're part of their genetic story!
why_it_matters: This discovery shows how the foods your ancestors ate can still affect your body today—every time you eat a potato, you are connecting to a deep family history of farming and survival.

background_read: Starch is a long chain of sugar molecules and needs special enzymes to be broken down into energy. The more copies of the AMY1 gene a person has, the faster and better this can happen in their mouth.

The Andes mountains in South America are one of the world's oldest centers of farming, with potatoes first planted there over 7,000 years ago. Indigenous communities there still grow hundreds of potato varieties.

Evolution doesn't only happen over millions of years—it can speed up when a new food source changes people's survival odds. A similar story is how some human groups developed genes to digest milk after they started herding cattle.
Article_Structure: WHO: Indigenous people in the Peruvian Andes and the scientists studying their genes.
WHAT: They carry more copies of the AMY1 gene, which helps break down starchy foods like potatoes better than most people.
WHERE: In the high Andes mountains of Peru, and compared with Maya people in Mexico who don't have the same extra copies.
WHY: To show that farming potatoes thousands of years ago changed human evolution, giving an advantage to those with more AMY1 copies.
